## \'Bath Brick\' {#1865}

**Description:** \'Bath Brick\' made her first appearance in  <i>MP</i> in May 1876 as a participant in the [[other:116]Spider] competitions, when she was commended for a life of the Cid.  In June 1876 she appears as ‘A Bath Brick’.  Requested to describe ‘A  Parish Church’  she chose Clevedon (September 1876): \'on one of the rounded headlands of the Bristol Channel, between Brean Down and Portishead, nestles the old parish church of C____ , dedicated to St. Andrew.\'  
In March 1879 she described Wrington in answer to \'Describe the most interesting place in your neighbourhood\'.  Therefore it seems reasonable to assume that she resided in north Somerset.  As well as being a regular contestant in the Spider competitions, Bath Brick was also a frequent correspondent of the magazine. She is mentioned in the poem written by Mary Anderson Morshead to commemorate the ending of the Spiders in March 1887.  Subsequently she took part in the Debateable Ground essay society. Her last appearance was in September 1896.

As to her identity, one possibility is that she was Emma Caroline Scarth (Bath 1850-?1921), younger daughter of the Rev. Harry Scarth, Rector of Wrington.

##      Charles Warren Adams {#12}

**Dates:**  (1833-30 July 1903)  
**Description:**   animal rights campaigner  

He married, first (1861), Georgina Alethe Polson (b.1838), daughter of the Rev.

Hugh Polson and Georgiana, only child of Charlotte Yonge and her first husband Captain George Crawley, and therefore CMY’s first cousin once removed.  (Mrs Crawley was CMY's aunt and godmother and married secondly the Rev Thomas Jones, Rector of Exeter College Oxford).

The Polsons had other children: (Arthur b. 1831/2, George b. 1833/4, Rosalia b.1834/5 and Catharina K. b. 1835/6).

Adams married secondly (24 June 1885), in the teeth of her family, the Hon.

Mildred Mary Coleridge (1847-14 January 1929).

For his involvement in brawling during a church service at St.

George in the East, in defence of the innovations introduced by the vicar, see The Times (11, 14 April 1860). [LG 1952 Woollcombe Adams of Anstey Hall; 1841, 1851, 1861 censuses at www.ancestry.co.uk]

##      Georgina Alethe Adams {#13}

**Dates:**  (1838-?1880)   
**Description:** first cousin once removed to CMY, first wife of Charles Warren Adams  

The Times (11 January 1862) reported the marriage 'at Cape-town, cape of good Hope, Charles Warren Adams, Esq, son of the late Mr.

Serjeant Adams to Georgiana Alethe, youngest daughter of the Rev.

Hugh Polson.' The death of a Georgiana Alethe Adams aged 2 was registered in Fulham in 1880.

According to the Bristol Mercury and Daily Post (24 November 1884) Charles Warren Adams stated in court that he had lived happily with his wife who had died of cancer.

He had always supported his daughter.

The refusal of the Bishop of Cape Town to marry them was a mistake, and he had afterwards been reconciled to her family.

Charlotte A. R.

Adams is boarder in New Shoreham west Sussex in the 1891 census; visiting an old lady in Brighton in 1901.

##     Alethea Anderson Morshead {#27}

**Dates:**  (28 March 1815-22 July 1863)  
**Description:**  cousin of CMY  

The eldest daughter of the Rev.

John Yonge of Puslinch and Alethea Henrietta Bargus, she married (1845) John Philip Anderson Morshead of Widey Court, her second cousin, whose paternal grandmother was Elizabeth Yonge of Puslinch.

They had six sons.

She and her younger sister Anne were known as ‘great A and little a’, after a nursery rhyme.  [LG 1871 Morshead]

##      Anne Elizabeth Mary Anderson Morshead {#28}

**Dates:**  (1845/6-1928)  
**Description:**  missionary and schoolmistress  

Always called Mary, she was the daughter of Pentire Anderson Morshead and Charlotte Story; her paternal grandmother was a Yonge which made her a cousin of CMY.

She joined the Gosling Society as ‘Bog Oak’ and was one of the liveliest contributors to The Barnacle, she left when she went to South Africa to do missionary and social work in 1868; she later wrote a history of the Universities Mission to Central Africa 1859-1896 (1897) and  A Pioneer and Founder . . .

Robert Gray, first Bishop of Cape Town (1905).

She  also edited Eikon Basilike (1887).

For many years, from at least 1881, she was a matron at Marlborough St Giles Industrial School for Girls, Andover.

Many of her contributions to MP are signed ‘Bog Oak’.

Jackson’s Oxford Journal (30 May 1891) reports her speaking at a GFS conference as a member of the committee for the Winchester Diocese.

She was first cousin to fellow-Goslings Mary Sunderland and Anne Baker.

##  The Rev.    Edmund Doidge Anderson Morshead {#42}

**Dates:**  (1849-1912)  
**Description:**  cousin of CMY, schoolmaster  

Third son of Rev.

John Philip Anderson Morshead and Alethea Yonge, he was a brilliant child and educated at Winchester and New College, Oxford 1867-72.

He got a double first and returned to serve as assistant master at Winchester College 1872-1904.

He married (1 Aug 1878) Mary, fourth sister of William Andrewes Fearon, headmaster of Winchester College 1884-91.

He died of General Paralysis of the Insane after having spent some months in Holloway Sanatorium [Winchester College Register;  Wainewright, Winchester College; ODNB; LG 1871 Morshead; Hants RO MS 67M922W/82/21]

##  The Rev.    John Philip Anderson Morshead {#43}

**Dates:**  (<i>c</i>.1809-7 Sept 1881)  
**Description:**  cousin of CMY  

He matriculated from Exeter Coll 1827 and from 1854 was Vicar of Salcombe Regis.

His grandmother was Elizabeth Yonge, sister of the Rev.

Duke Yonge, Vicar of Cornwood, so he and his brother Captain Pentyre Anderson Morshead were cousins of the Yonges of Puslinch and of CMY.

He married (1845) his second cousin Alethea Yonge (1815-1863), eldest daughter of the Rev.

John Yonge of Puslinch.

## Elizabeth Anderson Morshead {#1716}

**Description:** cousin of CMY  

Elizabeth Yonge, sister of CMY\'s grandfather the Rev.

Duke Yonge, married a local landowner, Philip Morshead of Widey Court, Egg Buckland, Plymouth.

They had an only daughter Elizabeth Morshead, who married Colonel Anderson and had 11 children called Anderson Morshead.

Of these the heir, the Rev.

John Philip Anderson Morshead married (1845)his second cousin Alethea Yonge of Puslinch, Pentire was the father of Mary Anderson Morshead.

Their sister Elizabeth Morshead, referred to by Anne Yonge, died in Devon in 1849. [Burke LG 1871; death register]

He was a brother of Fulbert Archer and the Rev.

Charles Harward Archer. [LG 1952 Archer of Trelaske]

##      Maria Georgina Archer Houblon {#50}

**Dates:**  (b. 1853)  
**Description:**  member of the Gosling Society  

Daughter of the Rev.

Thomas Archer Houblon (1808-1874) and Eleanor Deedes (d.1865).  A Gosling as Polypodium, she lived in December 1876 at Peasmore Rectory, Newbury.

Her father had been one of W.J.

Butler's curates at Wantage;  her only brother, the Rev.  T. H.

Archer Houblon (1849-1933) succeeded him as Vicar of Wantage, 1881-1907, and Maria kept house for him.

She became an Associate of the Wantage sisterhood in 1870.

Of their three sisters Eleanor (d. 1917) became an associate in 1866;  Sophia (1844-1927) became a professed sister of the community in 1878 and Reverend Mother 1912-1920; and Louisa Margaret (d. 1924) became an associate in 1871, professed sister in 1880 and Reverend Mother of the daughter house of the Holy Rood, Worthing.

They were cousins of other Goslings Elisabeth Forbes and Rachel Deedes and were also related to the Bramstons [LG 1952, Lady Anne Archer Houblon, The Houblon Family;  Wantage archives;  WWW;  Journal of Clarissa Trant]

##      James John Arnold {#62}

**Dates:**  (b. Peckham 1834/5)  
**Description:**  of Boyatt, surveyor and engineer  

He married, first, Sarah (Vine) Arnold (Otterbourne 1821/2-1896).

In the 1861 census she is a spinster farmer of 39 with a companion niece Marianna Vine (b.1843/4) and he is her boarder, aged 26.

He married, secondly in Chelsea in the fourth quarter of 1896, Ellen Vine.

He was keeping a hotel in Colchester with his wife Ellen (b.

Hargham, Norfolk 1853/4) in 1901.

However, since his second wife seems to be the Ellen (Drane) Vine (b.

Hargham, Norfolk 1853/4), widow and milliner, living with her father in London in 1881 and 1891, it looks as if CMY’s suspicions that he had married within the forbidden limits were unfounded.

Marriage with a deceased wife’s niece was illegal in England and Wales until the passing of the Marriage (Prohibited Degrees) Relationship Act (1931).

##      Mary Bargus {#103}

**Dates:**  (1759?-1843)  
**Description:**  maternal grandmother of CMY  

Coleridge states, [Life](../others.html#40), 154 that CMY\'s grandmother died in 1848.

However, it seems more probable that she died in 1843, when the death was registered in Winchester of a person of that name.

She was daughter of the Rev.

Thomas Kingsman (1717-1779), Vicar of Botley, and married (1792), as his second wife, the Rev.

Thomas Bargus. \'I think she was 89\' when she died, wrote CMY.

The IGI records the christening of a Mary Kingsman at Botley in 1751, which would make her about 92 in 1843, and 44 at the time of FMY\'s birth in 1795.

Her father\'s death is recorded in the Town and Country Magazine (1780), 55.

## Charlotte Bargus {#1660}

**Dates:** b.1761  
**Description:** great-aunt of CMY

## Richard Bargus {#1661}

**Dates:** <i>c.</i>1722-1805  
**Description:** great-grandfather of CMY  

CMY describes him as \'a naval officer, who after sailing round the world with Lord Anson, had settled at Fareham, in Hampshire\' (Coleridge, Life 4).

He died in his 83rd year at Fareham (Gentleman’s Magazine, 1805, 389).

He married, first (Rowner 1745), Frances Eyer and, secondly (Fareham 1759), Ann Lock.

His second wife’s death is also recorded in the Gentleman’s Magazine (1814) 87.

According to the Hampshire Allegations for marriage licences they were 36 and 25 at marriage.

It appears from the IGI that the Rev.

Thomas Bargus (christened Fareham 1753) and Mary (Bargus) Bogue were the children of his first marriage, Sophia (Bargus) Leeke, Charlotte Bargus and John Lock Bargus (b. 1762/3) of the second.

There may have been other children.

## John Lock Bargus {#1662}

**Dates:** 1762/3-1786  
**Description:** great-uncle of CMY  

Son of Richard Bargus and Ann Lock, and half-brother of CMY’s grandfather the Rev.

Thomas Bargus. CMY in Coleridge, Life, 6 states that he died in the same epidemic as Lord Brooke (1772-1786), son of the 2nd Earl of Warwick and his first wife Georgiana Peachey (whose father Lord Selsey was Thomas Bargus’s patron).

John Lock Bargus appears in Alumni Oxonienses and Register of Gray’s Inn.

## Cordelia Bargus [formerly Colborne] {#1700}

**Dates:** (1751-1791)  
**Description:** first wife of CMY\'s grandfather  

No relation to CMY, this lady is all the same the key to the complex cousinhood which surrounded her.

She had two children, John and Cordelia Anne, by her first marriage to Samuel Colborne.

She then married the Rev.

Thomas Bargus, and died giving birth to their daughter Alethea Henrietta Bargus.

He remarried, and had a daughter, CMY\'s mother Frances Mary Bargus.

Cordelia Colborne married the Rev.

Duke Yonge.

Alethea married the latter\'s cousin the Rev John Yonge.

John Colborne married Elizabeth Yonge (sister of the Rev.

John Yonge).

Lastly, Frances married William Crawley Yonge (brother of the Rev.

Duke Yonge).

Charles Barter, Vicar of Sarsden, he was educated at Eton and Merton College Oxford, and became Vicar of Shipton-under-Wychwood in 1868. [Eton Register; Alumni Oxonienses]

##     Catherine Barter {#116}

**Dates:** (b.1818/9)  
**Description:** traveller and schoolmistress  

The daughter of the Rev.

Charles Barter, Rector of Sarsden, and niece of the Rev.

Robert Speckott Barter, she seems to have lived near her brother the Rev.

Henry Barter, Vicar of Shipton-under-Wychwood, and run (in 1871) a small school, whose pupils included a South African ward named Salome Melango. CMY calls her ‘Kate Barter’ and refers to her ‘young Zulus’.

She is not to be confused with her sister-in-law Elspeth Catherine ‘Kitty’ (Moberly) Barter, or with her first cousin Katherine Mary (Barter) Wordsworth.

She was the author of an anonymous travel book Alone among the Zulus: The narrative of a journey through the Zulu country, South Africa.

By a plain woman (London: SPCK 1866) and has an entry in S. O.

Spencer, British settlers in Natal, 1824-1857: A Biographical Register (2001).

She was born at Broadstone, Oxfordshire.

##     Jemima Blackburn {#159}

**Dates:**  (1823-1909)  
**Description:**  artist and naturalist  

Jemima (Wedderburn) Blackburn (1823-1909), a Scottish naturalist and painter, met CMY through [Frederic Rogers](../persons.html#1252) (1811-1889), later Lord Blachford, a Devon Tractarian who was married to her cousin Georgina Colvile (d.1900).

Blackburn’s memories of CMY are printed in Robert Fairley, [Jemima: Paintings and Memoirs of a Victorian Lady](../others.html#63) (Edinburgh : Canongate, 1988), 128: ‘Charlotte Yonge was a friend of the Rogers and was asked to stay while I was visiting them.

It was a very small house and we were lodged in two little garrets next one another, and used to brush out our hair together before going to bed, and so soon became friends.

She was very good looking with dark hair and fine eyes, spoke pleasantly and was a little above middle height.

We talked of many things. I found her not at all formidable, as one feared she might be, being so well informed; one might almost say learned. . . . I kept up the friendship as long as she lived, and got a good many letters from her while I was illustrating her books.’ She married Hugh Blackburn, Professor of Mathematics at Edinburgh University.

Jemima Blackburn discovered the habits of the cuckoo.

##   Mary Elizabeth Bromfield {#162}

**Dates:** 1824/5-1888  
**Description:** contributor to <i>MP</i>   

The identity of this person is slightly puzzling, though CMY called her one of \'my crack authors\'.

The most likely candidate seems to be Mary Elizabeth (Mills) Bromfield (Harrow 1824/5-1888 Newton Abbot), daughter of the Rev.

Dr William Mills, master of Exeter Grammar School, in 1861 living with an engineer brother in Canterbury.

She married (Canterbury 23 Sept 1862) the Rev.

Henry Bromfield, Vicar of Blockley, and was living with him there 1871.

In 1881 she was a widow with an aged spinster sister-in-law at Fladbury House, Pershore, the address with which she corresponds with MP.

She was probably the Mary E.

Bromfield, author of SPCK tales, Female Christian Names &c., in COPAC.

Another possibility is that she is also the contributor to Biographies of Good Women described as ‘the author of Magdalen Stafford’.

That novel, Magdalen Stafford, or, A Gleam of Sunshine on a Rainy Day (1857) and the same author’s The Home Life of English Ladies in the XVII Century (1860), may be Mrs Bromfield’s work.

##     Catherine Anna Mona Brougham {#207}

**Dates:**  (1804/5-1892)  
**Description:**  contributor to <i>MP</i> (1888)  

MS Girton College, Cambridge, To A.D.

Innes (9 June 1888), identifies the contributor of an article signed \'C.A.W.B.\' as \'Mrs Brougham/ Castlehaven Rectory/ Castletownsend\'.

The article is signed ‘C.A.W.B.’, and refers to ‘my mother, Lady M.’ and to the author as ‘aged’.

The initials were evidently misprinted, and the author Catherine Anna Mona Brougham (1804/5-1892), widow of the Rev.

Henry Brougham (d.1831), Rector of Tallow, and daughter of Sir John Macartney and his second wife Catherine Burgh.

Two other articles appeared in the Monthly Packet in 1889 over the initials \'C.A.M.B.\' Mrs Brougham was probably living with a clerical son, because E. Œ.

Somerville, who lived in Castletownsend, refers (10 September 1888) to \'a hideous tennis function at the Broughams.\' Selected Letters of Somerville and Ross ed. G.

Lewis (London: Faber 1989), 118.

Earlier \'Recollections of Parochial Work in Ireland\' had appeared in MP 1864-5, and the bank account shows payments to Mrs Brougham of £11 (20 April 1863); £10 (12 March 1864); £5 15 s. (29 August 1864); £8 (31 Jan 1865); £3.3s. (23 February 1866).

We are grateful to Mr Peter Wyly for supplying her dates of birth and death. [See also PB Brougham]

##  The Rev.    John Frederick Watkinson Bullock {#221}

**Dates:**  (1840-1918)  
**Description:**     

He succeeded his father and grandfather as Rector of Radwinter 1865-1916.

In 1902 he published the first three volumes of a projected six volume work called Daily Lections for every Morning and Evening throughout the Year (London: Rivington 1902).

Volume V of this work, described in his preface, was to have consisted of \'Lections on Anglican Worthies, arranged as additional Readings for Sunday\'.

These \'Biographies of Eminent Anglicans\' exist in MS and are catalogued under that name among the Bullock papers in the Bodleian Library, Oxford, but were never published, since no more of the Daily Lections ever appeared.

The biographies were contributed by various authors, including CMY, Elizabeth Rundle Charles and Florence Wilford. [ Burke LG 1862, Venn, Alumni Cantabrigienses. N.B.

Venn\'s statement that there is an obituary in the Guardian 11 April 1918 seems to be inaccurate.]

##      Anna Butler {#237}

**Dates:**  (b.1825/6)  
**Description:**  sister of the Very Rev. William John Butler, contributor to <i>MP</i> (1852)  

An obscure figure but an important early contributor to MP, she seems to have shared the family scholarly interests, being a student of German and Danish and author of a book CMY refers to as your 'Scandinavian book'  in early 1856.

The letters in the Fairclough collection are clearly addressed to a sister of William Butler, who had two, Frances, who married in 1843 and died in 1851, and Anna (b.1825/6), who was still alive in 1892, author of Likes and Dislikes: Some Passages in the Life of Emily Marsden (1858) and several other works published as by ‘The author of Likes and Dislikes', viz., Philip Bezant, or, Is Revenge Sweet? (1859), The Brotherhood of St.

John the Evangelist at Berlin (1859), Chilcote Park, or, The Sisters (1860) and The Post Office Window, Being a Tale of the Night School (1862).

The identification is confirmed by payments to Miss A.

Butler in the bank account.

##  The Rev.    Richard Carter Smith {#267}

**Dates:**  (1802-1864)  
**Description:**  perpetual curate of Charlton-next-Woolwich, father of Ann Carter Smith  

He was christened Morwenstow, Cornwall, 29 August 1802, son of William and Ann Smith; and married, at Campton, near Bedford, on 24 November 1825, Mary Williamson, daughter of the Rev.

Edmund (Boase has Edmond) Williamson (c.1760-1839), Rector of Campton with Shefford, Beds., and his wife Phoebe Riland.

Smith was admitted, late in life, a fellow commoner at Caius College, Cambridge in 1844, proceeded BA and MA in 1849 and 1860, was ordained deacon in 1848 and priest in 1849.

He served as curate of Sutton Coldfield, Warwickshire 1848-50, Pershore 1851-3, Stepney 1854-7, and Charlton-next-Woolwich from 1862, being appointed to the perpetual curacy of St.

Pauls Charlton.

He died aged 62 on 1 October 1864.

It looks as if Richard Carter Smith was emulating one of his brothers-in-law in retraining for the church in the crisis years of the early 1840s, and that after he was ordained he acted as curate to another brother-in-law for five years.

He has  BL or Copac entries but the Harvard library catalogue lists Richard Carter Smith, Reise i Norge 1838 overs av Johnny Johnsen (Oslo, Univertitesforl c.1976).

This corroborates the evidence that the Carter Smith family had spent time in Norway. [IGI; Alumni Cantabrigienses, there is a brief death notice in the Gentleman's Magazine.]

##    Eliza Callahan Cleveland {#307}

**Dates:**  (1839-1914)  
**Description:**  American correspondent of CMY  

She is described as contributing sketches of good works among negroes to Mission Life 1867.

She and her mother are mentioned as friends in Elizabeth Sewell\'s autobiography, which was probably how the correspondence with CMY arose.

She was the daughter of Sarah Paine Perkins and Henry Russell Cleveland (1808-1843) and was brought up in the New England political and literary establishment.

She was the niece of the art collector Edward Newton Perkins (1820-1899) and was travelling with him and her mother in Italy in 1859 when they were attacked by local revolutionaries, causing a diplomatic incident.

Eugene Hollahan \'Intertextual Bondings Between \"The Wreck of the Hesperus\" and \"The Wreck of the Deutschland\"\' Texas Studies in Literature and Language 33 (1991) discusses her correspondence with Longfellow which she communicated to CMY who published it in MP.

There is a large collection of the Cleveland and Perkins papers in the New York Public Library.

## Sarah Paine Cleveland {#1939}

**Dates:** (d.1893)  
**Description:** mother of Eliza Callahan Cleveland  

Mother and daughter were friends of Elizabeth Sewell\'s; see her autobiography (1907), 159, 208.

See also A Selection from the Writings of Henry R.

Cleveland, with a Memoir (Boston: private distribution 1844).

She married Henry Russell Cleveland (1808-1843) in 1838 and they had one daughter (b. 1839).

She was the sister of the art collector Edward Newton Perkins (1820-1899) and she and her daughter were with him in Perugia in 1859 when they were attacked by local revolutionaries, causing a diplomatic incident.

A large collection of their papers is in the New York Public Library.

If the book she sent CMY in 1874 was Nina Cole, Meditations on the Song of Songs (London: Hayes 1874), an anonymous volume identified by Halkett and Laing, that may have been her name. A person of this name was a committee member of the Church and Stage Guild (founded 1879).

Its objects, according to an advertisement in The Era (13 July 1879) were \'to promote religious and social sympathy between the members of the Church and of the Stage\'.

John Francis Cole, Vicar of Kirdford, near Petworth, Sussex, who was a subscriber to MP and appears in its correspondence column (December 1877) 592.

##      Alice Mary Coleridge {#327}

**Dates:**  (1846-1907)  
**Description:**  member of the Gosling Society, cousin of CMY  

Much the youngest daughter of Francis Coleridge (1794-1854); her mother sank into depression after her birth and she was brought up by her elder sister Harriet Duke (Coleridge) Lowe (b.1829/30), wife of the Rev.

Edward Clarke Lowe (1823-1912) one of the moving spirits in the Woodard Schools movement for the education of the middle classes.

She lived with them at The College, Hurstpierpoint, and was a Gosling as ‘Gurgoyle’ 1863-after 1869.

She became Lady Warden of St.

Anne's Abbot's Bromley, a Woodard girls' school, c. 1874 and spent the rest of her life there.

Her brother Arthur Duke Coleridge was father of Mary E.

Coleridge, the poet.

She was CMY's goddaughter.

It looks from the Barnacle as if she spent some time living with Mildred and/or Mary Coleridge.  [ODNB; Rice, Story of St.

Mary's Abbot's Bromley; Coleridge, Story of a Devonshire House]

##      Arthur Duke Coleridge {#328}

**Dates:**  (1830/1-1913)  
**Description:**  father of Mary Elizabeth Coleridge  

Third son of Francis Coleridge, solicitor, of Ottery (brother to Sir John Taylor Coleridge) he was the elder brother of Alice Mary Coleridge, and a cousin of Coleridge Patteson and Mary Coleridge.

His mother Frances Duke (Taylor) Coleridge was a first cousin of CMY’s grandfather the Rev.

Duke Yonge, so they were third cousins. [Obituaries Times 30, 31 October 1913]

##      Christabel Rose Coleridge {#329}

**Dates:**  (1843-14 Nov 1921)  
**Description:**  biographer of CMY  

Daughter of the Rev.

Derwent Coleridge (1800-1883), headmaster (1826-41) of Helston Grammar School, Principal (1841-64) of St Mark\'s College, Chelsea, and Rector (1864-80) of Hanwell, Middlesex, and his wife Mary Simpson Pridham;  she was granddaughter of S. T.

Coleridge.

The longest-serving member of the Gosling Society, she was called Chelsea Delf to 1863 and Chelsea China thereafter;  she acted as secretary and many members seem to have been recruited by her;  she was first cousin to Cobweb and Hedgerose; Ladybird, Gurgoyle, Pena and Cricket were more distant relations.

The move to Hanwell took place in August 1864.

In 1873 she was evidently helping her brother Ernest run a school in his house at Chiddingfold.

Contributor to (including Debatable Ground) and later editor of MP.

From 1890 she was editor of Friendly Leaves (Jan 1876 to June 1917) a magazine, originally edited by Anne Mercier, produced by the Girls\' Friendly Society (founded 1875).

Will proved £4615 [Hainton, Unknown Coleridge;  DNB; will]

She was an artist, and may have contributed illustrations to the Barnacle.

Unlike Christabel she was related to CMY, through her father, who was Sir John Taylor Coleridge\'s brother. [Hainton, Unknown Coleridge, Roels MSS genealogy]

##      Mary Frances Keble Coleridge {#351}

**Dates:**  (1824-25 March 1898)  
**Description:**  daughter of Sir [[person:344]John Taylor Coleridge], cousin and lifelong friend of CMY, member of the Gosling Society  

The intimacy between CMY and Mary Coleridge is not well documented because the letters to her were, Christabel Coleridge states, burnt in an accident, but she is very frequently referred to in letters to others.

Her 1845 engagement to Roundell Palmer, later 1st Earl of Selborne, was broken off, and she never married.

She was devoted to her niece Mildred, daughter of Lord Coleridge, and encouraged CMY to found the Gosling Society partly in order to find an outlet for Mildred\'s intellectual interests.

Her Gosling name was The Old Secretary, but when Mildred lost interest in the society, she did likewise.

She was devastated by the furore over Mildred\'s 1885 marriage to Charles Warren Adams, who had sued Bernard Coleridge for libel.

In the same year her brother Lord Coleridge had married Amy Lawford, who had previously lived as the wife of her first cousin, but had then had their Gretna Green marriage declared invalid.

It appears that Mary Coleridge, like CMY, consequently disapproved of the second Lady Coleridge, and deplored her influence on her husband. [PB: Coleridge, Story of a Devonshire House]

A portrait of her and her sister Alethea as girls sold in 2006 is illustrated at www.artnet.com/Artists/LotDetailPage.aspx?lot_id=5830456F7F89012700A33CFAA5D

##  Captain    Charles Francis Cromie {#386}

**Dates:**  (1858-1907)  
**Description:**  nephew-in-law of CMY  

He entered the 37th Hampshire Regiment in 1878; he became captain in 1884; went to Staff College 1890-1891; and retired from the army in 1892.

He married, first (1881) Mary Grace Webb Bowen, and had at least one son born in 1882.

He petitioned for divorce on the grounds of her adultery with Captain Coddington, RN, commander of the ship Duke of Wellington; this was granted 11 May 1892.

He married, secondly (1894), CMY’s niece Joanna Angela Yonge.

He served as Vice-Consul at Dar-al-Baida, Morocco, 1894-1899; and Algeciras, 1899-1902; and was Consul at Dakar and for the Republic of Liberia, 1902-1905.

The Who’s Who entry of his son by his first wife calls her Mrs Lennard; she seems to have remarried John Milner Lennard in 1905. [Daily News (12 May 1892); WWW C.F.

Cromie and Francis Cromie (1882-1918]]

##      Elizabeth A. Curteis {#395}

**Dates:**  (born Ireland 1840/1)  
**Description:** writer and possible contributor to <i>MP</i>  

The wife of the Rev.

George Herbert Curteis (1823/4-1894), head of Lichfield Theological College in 1861, Rector of Waldron, Sussex in 1881, chaplain of Royal Savoy Chapel in 1891, she wrote a life of Bishop Selwyn , and children\'s verse.

Another possible candidate for this Mrs Curteis is Frances Curteis (1816/7-1887), mother of Bessie Charlotte Curteis, a known contributor.

##      Elizabeth Charlotte Curteis {#396}

**Dates:**  (b.1845)  
**Description:**  contributor to <i>MP</i>  

This person was author, as Bessie C.

Curteis, of In the Marsh (SPCK 1876).

East Sussex Record Office MS AMS6128/3/27 is a letter (June 1875) from Bessie Charlotte Curteis to her father Edward Barrett Curteis of Leasam House, Rye, Sussex, stating that she has been offered £50 for the manuscript of her article in the Monthly Packet.

She was no doubt the \'B.C.C.\' who wrote \'On Dialect\' MP (February 1874) 171-184.

It therefore seems reasonable to assume that she is the \'Miss Curteis\' of Leasams to whom CMY was writing about \'your eagle and goose story\', in a letter probably dating from 1872.

Her mother Frances Curteis (1816/7-1887) might have been the Mrs Curteis to whom CMY addressed a letter of 1878, but Elizabeth A.

Curteis seems more plausible

## Mrs. Curteis {#2034}

**Description:** author of \'Mrs. Twitch\'  

\'Mrs.

Twitch\' was a story, signed R. L. C., published in MP (June 1869) 606-12, which gave rise to a query answered in (October 1869) 415.

Two later stories, also about Mrs Twitch and presumably by the same author, were \'Pin-Baskets\' (June 1875) 639-646, and \'True and Just in All My Dealings\' (September 1881) 300-3. \'St.

Canace\'s Jackdaw\' was a poem, published in MP (August 1869) 140-1.

The other stories mentioned in CMY\'s letter to Mrs Curteis have not been traced.

##      Louisa Dundas {#454}

**Dates:**    
**Description:**  contributor to <i>MP</i> (1890, and probably also 1887)

From the obituary \'L.

Dundas\' contributed to MP (1887) (2) 151, of her youngest sister Adela Dundas (1840-1887) it is clear that she cannot be Katharine Louisa Dundas (b. 1849), youngest sister of Mary Frances Dundas.

It is also clear from this source that her father died in 1883.

She was probably the Louisa Dundas christened in February 1834, daughter of William Pitt Dundas (d.1883), Registrar General of Scotland, and his cousin and wife Mary Strange, whose daughter Adela was christened 1840 (there were several other children too).

##      Mary Anne Dyson {#464}

**Dates:**  (28 March 1809-29 Sept 1878)  
**Description:**  writer and schoolmistress

Charles Dyson, Rector of Dogmersfield, until his death in 1860, and latterly at Church Crookham.

Her will was proved by her nephew the Rev Francis Dyson, estate under £10,000.

She was an invalid ‘confined her to a sofa and latterly even to her bed’ ; author of Conversations with Cousin Rachel, Little Alice and her Sister, The White Kitten, Out in the Dark, Ivo and Verena, [wills index, obit MP (1878, 2, 521-5]

##      Marion Finlaison {#512}

**Dates:**  (b. London 1834/5-1914)  
**Description:**  schoolmistress, subeditor of <i>MP</i>  

CMY\'s neighbour Marion Finlaison (1834/5-1914) is described in Coleridge, [Life](../others.html#40), 272, 280.

She ran a small boarding-school in Otterbourne and acted as sub-editor of MP.

Although Marion is what she wrote on the census forms, it appears she was actually baptised Catherine Jane.

She was the daughter of William Finlaison (1789-1852), Captain RN (he was brother of the actuary and was on the Beagle, briefly also governor of Ascension I) and Mary Anne Ovenden.

In 1861, calling herself Marion C. C [or J?].

Finlaison, she was living with her mother in the household of her sister Mary Isobell (1819-1900) and brother-in-law, the Rev. [Henry Jenner](../persons.html#758) (1820-1898), Rector of Preston, Kent.

Jenner was later made Bishop of Dunedin New Zealand (though rejected as too High) and Bishop of the Eglise Catholique Gallicane.

Marion Finlaison acted as subeditor of the MP and ran a small boarding school in Otterbourne from late 1870s, probably successor of the school run by Mary Adams.

She was evidently known by her family as Kate.

She lived at Wingham between Preston and Otterbourne. [Not in PO Directory 1875, listed in White\'s Directory 1878; Finlaison letters; geocities.]

##      Margaret Gatty {#549}

**Dates:**  (1809-1873)  
**Description:**  children’s writer and naturalist  

She married (8 July 1839) the Rev.

Alfred Gatty (1813-1903), Vicar of Ecclesfield; she was the mother of Juliana Horatia (Gatty) Ewing, and a contributor to MP (1857-69).

Gatty’s Aunt Judy’s Tales (1859) and Aunt Judy’s Letters (1862) were made up of contributions to the MP from 1858 to 1865. \'Aunt Judy\' was there represented as an older sister telling stories to her younger brothers and sisters, and was based on Gatty’s daughter [Juliana Horatia Gatty](../persons.html#494) (1841-1885), later Ewing, who herself began to contribute to the MP in 1861.

In 1866 Gatty began to edit a periodical for George Bell called [Aunt Judy’s Magazine](../others.html#54) and most of the later fiction of both mother and daughter appeared there.

The most likely candidate seems to be the third sister, Charlotte Esther Sophia Guille Other possibilities among the sisters are the eldest, Louisa Margaret A.

##  The Rev.    George Collyer Harris {#625}

**Dates:**  (Toronto, Canada 1833-4 May 1874)  
**Description:**  step cousin of CMY, contributor to <i>MP</i> (1869, 1870)  

The only son of the Rev.

Joseph H.

Harris’s first marriage to Charlotte Collyer.

She died, probably in child birth in 1834 in Canada and Joseph remarried (1837) Jane Yonge, sister of Uncle Yonge, who had accompanied her sister Lady Seaton to Canada.

George Harris was born in Toronto and educated at Harrow and Exeter College Oxford (BA 1856, MA 1858) He served as curate of Chipping Campden 1857-9, then Tor Mohun 1859-65; he was Vicar of St Luke\'s, Torquay from 1865 until his death.

He died at his parents\' house, Sorel, Torquay.

He married (London 1865) Percy [sic] Primrose (b.

Quebec 1839/40) and had Edward Percy Harris (b.1866/7-?d.1872),  George Montagu Harris (b.1869) and Mary J Y Harris (b.1871), the latter the biographer of Frances Mary Peard. [Boase supp; 1871, 1901, 1881 census, information from Ian Yonge.]

##      Sophia Jane Harrison {#638}

**Dates:**  (1826-1891)  
**Description:**  wife of Thomas Elliot Harrison  

Daughter of the Rev.

John Collinson, Rector of Boldon, and Amelia King, she married (6 January 1859), as his second wife, Thomas Elliot Harrison (1808-1888), of Whitburn, Sunderland-on-Wear, the distinguished railway engineer and entrepreneur, see ODNB.

They had two sons and four daughters; one of the latter, Katharine Charlotte Harrison, was CMY’s goddaughter. CMY stayed with them at Whitburn and at their house in Paddington in London.

See the dedication of Grisly Grisell.

Sophia Harrison’s sister Thomasine Septima Collinson married the Rev.

Henry de Winton (d. 1895), Archdeacon of Brecknock, and is probably the Mrs de Winton mentioned in the letter to her.

However, Julia Cecilia Collinson (1812-1876) who married first (1831) Walter de Winton, ne Wilkins (d.1840), and secondly (1857) William Stretton (d 1868) , whose biography CMY wrote in Women Novelists of Queen Victoria’s Reign, was also a member of this family, another sister of Mrs Harrison. [Sutherland, Longman Companion, under Stretton; LG 1952 de Winton; ODNB T. E.

Harrison; PB 1914; Coleridge, Life 31-2; corr. N&Q (1908)]

##  The Rev.    William George Henderson {#678}

**Dates:**  (1819–1905)  
**Description:**  contributor to <i>MP</i> (1862)  

He married (1852) Jane Melville (d. 1901); he was contributor to MP (1862) as W. H.; he may also be the contributor of 1866 with the same signature.

He was one of the editors of the Surtees Society’s publications, and was evidently the author of the series of articles ‘Notes on the Folk Lore of the North of England’ which appeared in the Monthly Packet in 1862 signed ‘W. H.’.

His ODNB entry implies that he did not move from Jersey to become headmaster of Leeds Grammar School until 1862, but this letter suggests that he was already residing in the north of England in the previous year.

##      Edith Sophia Jacob {#749}

**Dates:**  (1836-1918)  
**Description:**  contributor to <i>MP</i> (1867)  

Daughter of the Venerable Canon Philip Jacob (1802/3-1884), rector from 1831 of Crawley with Hunton, north-west of Winchester, and canon and (from 1860) Archdeacon of Winchester, and his wife, Anna Sophia (1807?-1857), eldest daughter of the Hon.

Gerard Thomas Noel, canon of Winchester.

The parents were married in 1832.

Edith, according to her brother Edgar 'was left in February, 1857, by the death of her mother . . . the eldest daughter of seven surviving children.'1 There were four sons and three daughters of the marriage; a son who went into the army; another son, who went into the navy, either one of whom may have been Eustace Wilberforce Jacob (b.?1834-9 July 1871), SPG missionary in South Africa; Isabel Margaret (b. 1840/1); Edgar (1844-1920); and Ernest Henry (1849-1894), MRCS.

Their father had been brought up partly in Guernsey, and his father John Jacob (1765-1840) had published a history of the island.

The family also had many connections with India.

Edith lived at home, but became seriously ill early in 1868; her disease was described as 'congestion of the spine' and she spent most of the rest of her life in varying degrees of invalidism.

During this first attack, according to her brother, she reflected on the contribution which invalids could make to the life of the Church.

The result of this was a paper 'Thoughts on invalid life' published at the suggestion of CMY and reviewed by her in the Church Quarterly Review.

This resulted in the foundation of the 'Society of Watchers and Workers', an organisation to which Edith Jacob devoted her energies for the rest of her life, and of whose privately printed journal, the Watchword, she was editor.

This periodical ran 1880-1972; the BL has only odd volumes, but there is a complete run in Lambeth Palace Library.

The BL's copies are bound with interesting rolls of members of the society; CMY is listed as a member of the executive committee.

The activities of the society, which included support for homebound 'invalids of the cultured classes', enabling them to direct their energies in prayer and fundraising for charitable objects, are described in more detail in Kathleen Alice Orr, Letters (1907, 1909), a privately printed memoir of a deceased watcher with a memoir by Edith Jacob.

The Watchers were especially keen on missions.

##  Mrs     Jewell {#767}

**Dates:**    
**Description:**  inhabitant of Otterbourne, her husband invalid or workshy  

Perhaps Mary Jewell (b. 1852/3) wife of William Jewell, of Otterbourne, labourer, and mother of Rose (b.1877/8) and Percy (b. 1879/80).

She may also be the Mrs Jewell who was one of CMY’s tenants in 1896.

Probably the same Mrs Jewell was working for Miss Finlaison in 1901.

##  The Rev.    Charles Alexander Johns {#769}

**Dates:**  (1811-1874)  
**Description:**  naturalist  

He taught at Helston Grammar School, when Derwent Coleridge was headmaster, and later ran a prep school at Winton House, Winchester.

He was founder and president of the Winchester Literary and Scientific Society.

He married (1843) Ellen Julia Field (b.

Bath 1821/2) Beenham in 1851 census, Watford in 1861.

His father was a Plymouth banker, whose firm had collapsed in 1825.

His most famous book was the very popular Flowers of the Field (1851). [ODNB]

##      Charles Henry Johns {#770}

**Dates:**  (1844-1915)  
**Description:**  son of the Rev. Charles Alexander Johns  

Eldest son of Charles Alexander Johns, he was educated at Rugby and Oriel College, Oxford, and taught at Winton House until after his father’s death, later at other schools.

In 1886 married Mary Emily Chalk who ran a school for girls at Lydney which they moved to Hendon.

He is mentioned in his mother’s will, along with his sister Katie, as having brought her to poverty.[Alumni Oxonienses, information from Melissa Hardie]

##      Edward Francis Johns {#771}

**Dates:**  (April 1861-1948)  
**Description:**  second son of the Rev. Charles Alexander Johns  

He was at Bradfield January 1879-July 1880, then an exhibitioner of Exeter College, Oxford (BA 1884), headmaster of Winton House Prep School 1895.

He married Violet Marsham in 1910 and had no children. [Alumni Oxonienses, Bradfield College Register]

##      Ellen Julia Johns {#772}

**Dates:**  (Bath 1821-1895 Winchester)  
**Description:**  wife of the Rev. Charles Alexander Johns  

She married (Chelsea 1843) the Rev.

Charles Alexander Johns, naturalist and schoolmaster.

She seems to have been related to the Keary sisters, possibly through their mother, daughter of Hall Plumer of Bilston Hall, brother of Sir Thomas Hall Plumer. [1881 census; information from Melissa Hardie; census]

##      Priscilla Hannah Johnston {#775}

**Dates:**  (1842-1912)  
**Description:**  campaigner for Balkan minorities  

Coming from a family with a strong record on anti-slavery campaigning and prison visiting, she ran a school for Christian girls in Sarajevo with Paulina Irby, closed it in 1875 as a result of uprising and succoured refugees on Slavonia border.

The letter to her (1876) concerns taking clothes to Herzegovina for Serbian refugees; she returned to England 1885. [Paulina Irby and Johnston’s namesake mother have ODNB entries ;D.

Anderson, Miss Irby and Her Friends.]

##      Anna Maria Keary {#793}

**Dates:**  (3 March 1825-March 1879)  
**Description:**  writer,  contributor to <i>MP</i> (1865-76)  

Sixth child of the Rev.

William Keary, Rector of Bilton, perpetual curate of Sailcoates, and rector of Nunnington.

Her mother was daughter of Hall Plumer of Bilston Hall, brother of Sir Thomas Hall Plumer.

She and her sister Eliza went to live in Addison Road 1854, later in Bedford Gardens.

She worked in a children\'s hospital and was rather deaf.

They seem to have been related to the Johns family. IIn 1873 she seems to have taken part in the essay-writing part of the Gosling Society, but if she had a sobriquet it is not known. [Eliza Keary Memoir of Annie Keary;Vital records index for death]

##      Edith Emma Knight {#822}

**Dates:**  (4? March 1851-1936)  
**Description:**  member of the Gosling Society, daughter of the Very Rev. William John Butler  

Known as Emma Butler, she was the daughter of CMY’s great friends the Rev.

William Butler, Vicar of Wantage and later Dean of Lincoln and his wife Emma Barnett (1813-1894). A member of the Gosling Society as ‘Frog’, she married (Oct-Dec 1877) as his third wife, Edward Lewis Knight (1817-1882), of Hornacott Manor, Cornwall.

She was an associate of the Wantage sisterhood.

She inherited her aunt Elizabeth Barnett's letters from CMY and lent them to both Coleridge and Romanes. [LG 1906 Knight of Wolverley, will, Life and Letters of Dean Butler; Memoirs of Arthur John Butler]

##      Charlotte Latham {#840}

**Dates:**  (b.Sussex 1801/2)  
**Description:**  mother of Margaret Roberts  

According to George Ormerod, Parentalia (privately printed 1851), she was the daughter of the Rev.

Henry Warren, prebendary of Bangor.

She married, first, the Rev.

Ellis Roberts, Vicar of Llanynys, and, secondly (1848), as his second wife, the Rev.

Henry Latham.

She was living with the latter at Fittleworth in the 1851 census; at Tormoham, Torquay in 1871 with her stepdaughter Dina [sic] Latham, daughter Margaret Roberts, and stepgranddaughters Margaret and Katharine Mary Hutchingstone, 11 and 7;  in the 1881 census again at Tormoham with Diana Latham and Margaret Roberts and granddaughter Helen M Latham, 13.

See under Grace Latham for the implication that there was a blood relationship between either Charlotte Latham or her first husband and some members of the Latham family.

##      Diana Latham {#841}

**Dates:**  (b 1824/5)  
**Description:**  daughter of the Rev. Henry Latham  

She was daughter of Latham and his first wife Maria Halliwell, and stepsister of Margaret Roberts.
[1851, 1871, 1881 census; George Ormerod, Parentalia (1851)]
Diana Latham contributed some reminiscences to the autobiography of her cousin the naturalist Eleanor Ormerod (1828-1901: Eleanor Ormerod, LL.D., economic entomologist: Autobiography and correspondenceedited by Robert Wallace (London : John Murray, 1904)

##      Mary Elizabeth Latimer {#846}

**Dates:**  (1822-1904)  
**Description:**  American historian, contributor to <i>MP</i> (1879-93)  

She lived in Baltimore, Maryland, and published two novels as Elizabeth Wormeley: Amabel: A Family History (1853) and Our Cousin Veronica, or, Scenes and Adventures Over the Blue Ridge (1855).

In the 1880s she began writing again, publishing three novels under the name Elizabeth Wormeley Latimer: Salvage (1880), My Wife and My Wife\'s Sister, 1881, and Princess Amélie: A Fragment of Autobiography (1883).

In 1888 she published three translations from the French: History of the People of Israel, by Ernest Renan, and For Fifteen Years and Steel Hammer, both by Louis Ulbach and in 1890 George Sand’s Nanon.

In the 1890s and early 1900s she published a series of books on the history of various European nations, and on the colonisation of Africa, three more translations and a final novel, Prince Incognito (1902).

##      Ann Catherine Lloyd {#887}

**Dates:**  (Helston 1847/8-1903 Benares)  
**Description:**  artist, member of the Gosling Society  

Known as Katie, she was an artist and illustrator, daughter of the Rev. [Charles Alexander Johns](../persons.html#769).

She was a Gosling as Kittiwake in 1864-5.

She married in 1873 the Rev.

John Henry Lloyd, curate of Wormleighton and subsequently Vicar of Fotheringay.

He was curate to the Rev.

William Harrison, Vicar of Wormleighton, who was married to Mary Kingsley (1852-1931), daughter of Charles Kingsley and a friend of Katie Johns.

Both marriages seem to have come to grief.

In 1891 she was living apart from her husband and was matron of Annie Besant’s Women’s Home at 193 Bow Road, a kind of club for girls in the East End, with a few resident matchmakers. A.H.Nethercot The First Five Lives of Annie Besant (Chicago, U of C P 1960) 337, calls her ‘Mrs Kitty Lloyd’ and describes her as ‘a devoted Theosophist’.

Later her health broke down and she was sent to Ceylon and then to Benares, where she ended her days as the much-loved Matron of the Central Hindu College Boarding House.

She is mentioned in her mother’s will (1895), along with her brother Charles, as having brought her to poverty.[ [census returns 1881, 1891; marriage index; clergy lists; Nethercot, First Five Lives of Annie Besant; Theosophical Yearbook 1933; Obituary in The Theosophist, 1903; info from Professor Joy Dixon]

##  The Rev.    John Henry Lloyd {#892}

**Dates:**  (b. Essex 1846/7)  
**Description:**  Vicar of Fotheringhay, husband of Katie Johns  

He was educated at Chichester Theological College 1869-71, deacon 1871, priest 1872, curate of St.

Michael Lichfield 1871-2, of Maulden, Ampthill 1875, of Clifton Biggleswade 1877-8.

He married (1873) Ann Catherine Johns.

He was curate in charge of Wormleighton 1880-1 and vicar of Fotheringay 1881-1890, but had no cure by the 1891 volume of Crockfords, and was perhaps living apart from his wife.

He disappears from the Clergy List c. 1900, reappears 1907, but is more continuous in Crockfords; he lived at 90 Canonbury Avenue until about 1933. [Crockfords, Clergy List, census returns 1871, 81, 91]

##      Amy Aubrey Locke {#893}

**Dates:**  (1881-1916)  
**Description:**  historian  

First holder of the Charlotte Yonge scholarship from Winchester High School, she was daughter of Alfred L.

Locke, head porter to Winchester College.

She is listed as a student at Somerville College Oxford in the 1901 census.

She published several works of history before her early death and was employed by the Central Office of the Victoria County History project.

She seems to have called herself Audrey in adult life.

For a description of how her substantial contribution to the Cornwall section Victoria History of the Counties of England remained unpublished owing to the dilatoriness of another contributor, see John Beckett, \'Canon Thomas Taylor of St.

Just and the Victoria County History in Cornwall, 1899-1938\' Journal of the Royal Institution of Cornwall (2011) 31-44, 38-9.

Probably more material on her professional career is to be found in the Victoria County History Archive, held by the Institute of Historical Research, University of London.

##      Maria Marriott {#958}

In the 1901 census they were living together at Eastleigh, and one of them must therefore be the Miss Marriott who organised the reprinting of Last Heartsease Leaves in 1900. [1851 census; birth, death index, 1881, 1891, 1901 censuses]

##      Blanche Catherine Medhurst {#988}

**Dates:**  (London 1848- Barnstaple 1925)  
**Description:**  social worker and contributor to <i>MP</i> (1873-5)  

She was daughter of Francis Hastings Medhurst (d.1852), of Kippax Hall, near Leeds, and Mary Anne Bushnan; a friend of Mrs Mercier and patroness of Emmeline Spratt.

She published a study of workhouses, The Idle Room (1886). [LG 1871, census] The 1861 census shows Mary Anne Medhurst with two other daughters and her mother Anne Bushman (d.1878) living at 29 Dorset Square; in the 1871 census Blanche is there too.

Hers is an odd story, because her father killed another boy while a private pupil at school and got three years for manslaughter in 1839, coming up before Mr Justice Coleridge; his grandfather, a rich stockbroker, had murdered his wife while insane and was at that time in an asylum. [Times].

She wrote an article in MP (1886) about the Associated Workers League, of which she was evidently a member.

##     Ellen J. Millington {#1000}

**Dates:** (b.1818)  
**Description:**   teacher and contributor to <i>MP</i>(1853-64)  

Ellen J.

Millington translated The Aesthetic and Miscellaneous Works of Frederick von Schlegel from the German in 1849 (reprinted a number of times up to 1891), Christian iconography, or, the history of Christian art in the Middle Ages by A.N.

Didron from the French in 1851, and herself wrote Heraldry in History, Poetry, and Romance (1858) and Characteristics of the Gods of Greece. A Manual for Schoolgirls (1867).

As well as the series of articles on heraldry, she contributed seven articles on ‘King Arthur and his Knights’ to the MP between 1861 and 1864.

Daughter of Henry Millington (b. 1790/1), attorney\'s clerk [1851 census, in Bristol], she is described by CMY as an invalid ex-governess; in the 1861 census she was living with her mother (father absent but evidently alive) Emma Millington (b.1794/5), her sister Anna Gerard (b. 1818/9), widowed by 1851 census, keeping a tiny school of three pupils in Westbury on Trym.

In the 1871 census her mother is Anna Millington, now a widow, Anna Gerard also now a widow, and the school bigger and occupying two houses in Clifton.

She was living at Hawarden, Wales, with Anna Gerard, in the 1881 census.

Her father is found in 1861 (not 1871) living with his son, the Rev.

Thomas Street Millington (1821-1906), curate, later vicar of Woodhouse, Leics., and a prolific author of theology and boys’ fiction.

##   Stephen Roger Moore {#1050}

**Dates:**  (fl. 1823-1845)  
**Description:** cousin-in-law of FMY  

The Mr Moore mentioned in the 1840s is assumed to be Stephen Roger Moore, who married (Otterbourne 1823) FMY\'s first cousin Mary Kingsman (b.c. 1785).

They evidently lived in or near Otterbourne.

##    Mary Moore {#1051}

**Dates:**  (b.<i>c.</i>1785)  
**Description:** cousin of FMY  

The Mr and Mrs Moore mentioned in these early letters are perhaps the same as Mrs More who gave warm shawls to Otterbourne schoolchildren in December 1844;  Mrs Moore sent a parcel 24 Sept 1846 including Mr Kingsman\'s chain.

All these references have therefore been rather boldly associated with Mary Kingsman, a niece of FMY\'s mother Mary (Kingsman) Bargus, daughter of her brother William George Kingsman (b.1755).

The younger Mary Kingsman married (Otterbourne 1823) Stephen Roger Moore.

In 1848 she proved the will of her uncle John Kingsman (1764-1848) who left legacies to her, FMY, JBY, CMY and the Rev.

Thomas Westcombe.

She can probably be identified with the Maria Kingsman mentioned in the CMY\'s autobiographical chapters (Coleridge, Life, 7), the orphan niece who was a member of the Bargus household during FMY\'s childhood.

Details of the descendants of CMY\'s great-grandfather the Rev.

Thomas Kingsman (1717-1779), Vicar of Botley, are at http://freepages.genealogy.rootsweb.ancestry.com/~kingsman/kingsman/england/indiI13063.html

##     Elizabeth P. Roberts {#1243}

**Dates:**    
**Description:**  contributor to <i>MP</i> (1852-9)  

The author of the ‘Garland for the Year’, who preserved the letters which shed such a useful light on the early history of MP, signed her contributions E. P. R. or Elizabeth P.

Roberts.

She may perhaps be identified with Elizabeth Piddocke Roberts (b.

Kingswinford, Staffs. 1821) who published a book of verse in 1845.

That person was the daughter of John Piddocke Roberts (b.1794/5) and his wife Susannah Maria Morris (b. 1789/90), who had been married at Kingswinford in 1819; he is described in the 1841 census of Armitage, Staffs. as a land agent, and in the 1851 Isle of Man census as a landed proprietor.

By 1861 Elizabeth and her widowed mother were staying in West Bromwich, and she is described as a governess.

Since the \'Garland\' author\'s father evidently died in 1859 it is likely they are one and the same.

According to the IGI records she was one of at least ten children, of whom several died young.

Survivors included Rebecca Surgy Roberts (b. 1831) who acted as a companion to a cousin in the Isle of Wight (1851, 1861 census), Phoebe Cordelia Roberts (1828-after 1881) and Martha Sarah Roberts (1835-1909) who married (1852) Thomas Oxenbould, a banker’s clerk.

Roberts’s ‘Garland for the Year’ may possibly be the ‘semi botanical papers’ of which CMY wrote ‘I used to repent - of admitting them’.

[1841 census, Armitage with Handsacre, Staffs.; parents Isle of Man 1851 census; 1861 census with cousin Lydia Morris, chemist, at West Bromwich; Oxenboulds, 1871, 1891 census, Handsworth; BMD indexes; IGI]

##      Margaret Eliza Roberts {#1244}

**Dates:**  (1833-1919 Montreux)  
**Description:**  author of <i>Mademoiselle Mori</i>  

She was educated by her stepfather, the Rev.

Henry Latham (1794-1866 ODNB);  she was a contributor to MP (1864-92).

Her most successful work was Mademoiselle Mori:  A Tale of Modern Rome (1860), which CMY encouraged Parker to print; she published as ‘the author of Mademoiselle Mori’. CMY had a plan to co-author German history with her; she suffered a strain of the hip in 1873; and lived in Torquay.

She has titles in the British Library Catalogue 1857-1901. A letter in the Bodleian from Roberts to Bullock calls Grace Latham her cousin, and perhaps there was a blood relationship with some of the Lathams. (ODNB; Blain, Feminist Companion; Mary Harris, Frances Mary Peard says she died at Territet]

Robertson compiled chiefly from letters and journals written to the late Bishop Mackenzie and his sisters (Cambridge: Deighton 1866) and she also figures in CMY’s [Pioneers and Founders, or, Recent Workers in the Mission Field](../books.html#90) (London: Macmillan 1871).

##  Captain    Raphael Semmes {#1273}

**Dates:**  (1809-1877)  
**Description:**  captain of the <i>Alabama</i>  

A confederate warship was built anonymously in the British shipyards at Birkenhead.

When the Unionist government discovered this they demanded that it be detained in the yard, but in 1862, on the pretext of a trial run, Semmes and his crew escaped with it to the Azores where it was armed and proceeded to do immense damage to Unionist shipping, to the commercial benefit of the British.

In 1864 the Alabama was sunk off Cherbourg but Semmes was picked up by an English yacht and brought to England. CMY referred to the Alabama affair disapprovingly in the Barnacle.

##     Mary Emily Simpson {#1326}

**Dates:** (1820-1884)  
**Description:** educational reformer  

The author of Ploughing and Sowing was the daughter of the Rev.

Francis Simpson, Vicar of Boynton, and of Anne Strickland (d.1868), daughter of Sir William Strickland, 6th Bt.

She was not exactly niece of Sir Henry Boynton 10th Bt. (1811-69) of Burton Agnes, as CMY says, but his first wife Louisa Strickland (d.1841) was her mother’s first cousin, and other marriages connected the two families.

He was probably FMY\'s first cousin, son (or perhaps grandson) of her father\'s aunt Mary (Bargus) Bogue.

##      Jane Mary Smith-Dampier {#1345}

**Dates:**  (1836/7-Dec 1906)  
**Description:**  novelist, neighbour of CMY  

Jane Mary Dampier and her sister Emily Dampier (b.1838/9) lived at Twyford House, Twyford.

This accounts for her visiting (1870) with Mrs Buston, the wife of the vicar of Twyford.

Jane married (1873) Alfred Fowler Smith and adopted the surname Smith-Dampier: she was the author of a novel, Journal of Lady Beatrix Graham (1870) which was published with an introduction by CMY.

Some of her work was published as by Mrs Fowler Smith.

In the 1871 census Jane Mary Dampier was living unmarried at Twyford House with her sister Emily Dampier (b.1838/9), describes her occupation as 'keeping things in order'.

By the time of her death she was calling herself Smith-Dampier.

They were daughters of John L.

Dampier and Margaret Dampier; he was Vice-Warden of the Stannaries, and died 1851-61. [COPAC; 1871 census; 1841 census; death register]

##      Anne Sturges Bourne {#1379}

**Dates:**  (1809-9 Dec 1891)  
**Description:**  landowner  

Daughter of William Sturges Bourne (1769-1845), she was a rich philanthropic spinster. A lifelong friend of [Mary Anne Dyson](../persons.html#464), they shared interests in educational and charitable work.

Their very copious correspondence, with much detail on Tractarian projects and much gossip, survives in Hampshire Record Office.

Together they encouraged the young CMY’s philanthropic and literary work.

Anne Sturges Bourne appears to have been the author of the review of My Life and What Shall I Do With It? which appeared in 1861. [Her death aged 92 was reported in the Daily News 15 Dec 1891]

## Maria Edith Walker {#2234}

**Dates:** (Middlesex 1843-1938)  
**Description:** correspondent of CMY  

The letters from CMY to Miss M. E.

Walker were presented to West Sussex Record Office in 1975 by the latter\'s niece Bertha Yeats, who was then 91. [Information from Alison McCann, West Sussex Record Office] Bertha Margaret F.

Yeats (1883-1976) was the daughter of the Rev.

George Yeats (b.

Yorks. 1826/7), Vicar of Heworth, York, and Rosa Bertha Walker (1852-1900).

Mrs Yeats\'s sister, Maria Edith Walker, was therefore the recipient of the letters from CMY.

The Walker sisters were the daughters of Francis Walker (1809-1874), entomologist, and his wife and cousin Mary Elizabeth Ford (b. 1814/15), daughter of John Ford of Ellel Hall, Lancashire and Elizabeth Lawson.

Francis Walker, son of John Walker (1766-1824) was a member of a family of rich and philanthropic brewers living at Arnos Grove, Southgate, Middlesex.

The Miss Lawrence referred to in the correspondence, grandmother of Maria Walker, who had been at school with Frances Mary Yonge, was perhaps the wife of John Walker.

##     Gertrude Walter {#1462}

**Dates:**  (Shotapoor 24 May 1849-20 May 1897)  
**Description:**  housemate of CMY, sister-in-law of JBY  

Daughter of Edward Walter and Mary Emma Coulthard.

Her sister Frances married (1858) CMY\'s only brother Julian Bargus Yonge.

She moved into Elderfield with CMY in about 1872.

Her illness began 8 years before 1871.
[Bombay Baptisms N/3/24/118; \'she would have been 48 on the 24th\']

CMY described her movingly in ‘Our Tender Ones’ Mothers in Council 9 (January 1899) 20-27, 26:

‘Let me draw the picture of a real invalid not long passed away.

She was a bright active girl of fourteen when rheumatic fever set in, followed by arthritis.

Gradually, during nearly twenty years, every power was taken from her; first one knee was affected, then the other, then she could no longer sit at the piano, she moved on crutches, and drove in a donkey chaise; but in time, always after severe illness and pain, these pleasures failed her, she could only be carried from one room to another or to church on a couch.

She lost her voice, and next the use of her right arm, and for several years was entirely confined to bed.’

##  Miss     Warren {#1476}

**Dates:**    
**Description:**    

The Miss Warren and Gundred referred to by CMY in 1900 were possibly Louisa Warren and her sister Gundred (b.

Shropshire 1822/3) who appear in the 1891 census living at Market Drayton, but not in any earlier one, though a Georgiana Gundred Warren (birth registered Market Drayton 1839) appears with oddly varying dates of birth in the census returns.

Unusual as Gundred is as a name, it was that of the wife (d.1085), of William de Warenne (d.1088), and therefore seems to have been chosen by people named Warren unexpectedly often.

##      Florence Wilford {#1520}

**Dates:**  (Woolwich 29 Feb 1836-?1897)  
**Description:**  novelist, contributor to <i>MP</i> (1866-83), member of the Gosling Society  

Daughter of Major-General Edmund Neal Wilford (1800-1881), RA, Governor of the Royal Military Academy, Woolwich, until his retirement, she was a Gosling as ‘Turkscap’ from June 1865; her address then was c/o Mrs Chrystall\'s,.

St.

Cross, Winchester.

In the 1851 census, she was 15 and was staying at Bromley Kent, in the company of Maria Cristall, whom CMY describes as her aunt.

In 1881 she and her elder sister Emma, 48, were living with their father in St.

Leonards; in 1891 she and Emma were staying in Bournemouth.

Her Royal Literary Fund file indicates that she had suffered from mental illness intermittently since 1883 and was in a private asylum in 1889 when CMY wrote a letter to them on her behalf. (Her application was refused on the grounds ‘authorship insufficient’, which seems rather harsh since she had published sixteen books since 1858.) CMY assured Bullock (16 March 1895) that she was well and at home with her sister.

She was probably the Florence Wilford who died at Keynsham, Glos. in 1897. [IGI; RLF application 2311, born at Woolwich]

## Lieutenant George Dobson Willoughby {#1904}

**Dates:** (1828/9-11 May 1857)  
**Description:** The text of his memorial in Bath Abbey is at http://glosters.tripod.com/IM8.htm

\'Sacred to the memory of George Dobson Willoughby, 1st Lieut. Bengal Artillery and Commissary of Ordnance at Delhi, aged 28 years. As a brave and zealous soldier he stood firm in defence of his post intrusted to him, and when resistance failed blew up the Delhi Magazine on 11 May 1857 to prevent its falling into the hands of the mutineers and rebels. Burnt and wounded he subsequently fell a prey to insurgents. This tablet is erected by his sorrowing relatives.\'

CMY included his story in <i>A Book of Golden Deeds</i>, having read about him in <i>The Times</i>.

## Julia Lucy Woodward {#1657}

**Dates:** Cheltenham 1850-1910  
**Description:** probably a member of the Spider Society as \'Bath Brick\'  

Daughter of Richard Woodward (d.1875), retired Bengal Civil Service, she lived in Bath in 1871 and 1881
and 1891 with her widowed mother at the Knoll, Clevedon.

She was a fellow
of the Royal Meterological Society, a member of the Ex Libris Society
(collecting bookplates), and a supporter of local history societies and
publications.

She contributed a memoir of her uncle Vincent Stuckey Lean to
his book on proverbs (1902-4).

She compiled the autograph album in which the
letters to Bath Brick were found; since Bath Brick is known to have lived
near Clevedon they were probably the same person.

He was second master of Winchester College 1835-1846, and author of Christian Boyhood at a Public School (1846).

He was first headmaster of Trinity College Glenalmond, 1847.

He married, secondly (28 October 1846), Katharine Mary Barter (d. 23 Apr 1897), eldest daughter of the Rev.

William Barter, Rector of Burghclere, and niece of Warden Barter; he had 12 children by his second marriage.

Like the Rt.

Rev.

Christopher Wordsworth, Bishop of Lincoln, he was a son of the poet’s brother Christopher, master of Trinity College, Cambridge. [ODNB]

##  The Rt. Rev.    Christopher Wordsworth {#1565}

**Dates:**   (1807-1885)  
**Description:**  Bishop of Lincoln  

He married (6 December 1838) Susanna Hatley Frere (1811-1884); he was father of Elizabeth Wordsworth, brother of the Rt.

Rev.

Charles Wordsworth, and nephew of the poet. [LG 1952, LG 1871]

##      Elizabeth Wordsworth {#1566}

**Dates:**  (23 June 1840-30 Nov 1932)

Daughter of the Rt.

Rev.

Christopher Wordsworth, she was appointed Lady Principal of Lady Margaret Hall in 1878.

She contributed a poem to MP in 1871 under the name \'VERITAS\' and probably was the author of another 16 poems which appeared under that pseudonym to February 1883.

[Battiscombe, Reluctant Pioneer]

She married (28 October 1846), as his second wife, the Rev.

Charles Wordsworth.

She is not to be confused with her cousin Kate Barter, or the latter’s sister-in-law, Kitty (Moberly) Barter.

##  The Rev.    Duke Yonge {#1599}

**Dates:**  (21 June 1823-7 Oct 1881)  
**Description:**  cousin of CMY  

The fourth and only surviving of the five sons of the Rev.

John Yonge of Puslinch, and Alethea Henrietta (Bargus) Yonge, he inherited Puslinch in 1877 (John, James, John Bargus and Edmund Charles having predeceased him).

He was curate of Newton Ferrars in 1849, and subsequently Rector of Newton Ferrars like his father.

He married (26 Aug 1862) Charlotte Cordelia Pode (1839/40-7 Sept 1929), who was his second cousin (she was CMY's first cousin).

He shared two of her eight great-grandparents, whereas he shared four of CMY's eight great-grandparents.

According to a letter of his youngest daughter Alethea’s, he had wished to marry CMY.

##  The Rev.    Duke Yonge {#1600}

Jan 15 1847 aged 19 years\']

## Dr.   John Francis Duke Yonge {#1622}

**Dates:** (1814-25 Dec 1879)  
**Description:** cousin of CMY  

The son of the Rev.

Duke Yonge, Vicar of Antony, he married first (Brussels 12 August 1839) a widow with two children, Elizabeth Alice (Holmes) Reed (1799/1800-1863) and, secondly (1864) Mary Jones.

He seems to have converted to Roman Catholicism.

For that reason he was not welcome at WCY’s funeral.

By his first marriage he had three sons, Francis Arthur Holmes Yonge, James Frederick Moore Yonge (b.

Coblentz 1841/2?) and Stephen Duke Yonge (Coblentz 1844/5-1914).

In the 1871 census he and his second wife are living in Cornwall with three small grandsons, born in Mauritius, and probably the children of Francis, who had gone to live there.

The two younger sons had moved to Melbourne, Australia, by 1864.

One of the \'grandsons\', Eugene Yonge (b.

Mauritius 1867/8) appears in the 1881 census in Plymstock with his uncle the Rev.

Theophilus Jones (1822/3-1886), Vicar of Bradstone, and as a medical student in the 1891 census. [census; Alumni Oxonienses An obituary of \'Eugene Stephen Yonge, M.D.Edin., Physician, Manchester Hospital For Consumption\' appeared in the The British Medical Journal 1 (Feb. 3, 1912), p. 280; advertisement Morning Post 16 April 1864, 1]

**Dates:**  (31 Jan 1830-17 October 1891)

He was a J.P. for Hampshire; sold Otterbourne House to Major Robert Scarlett in 1891 and died ‘a few days later’ (John Keble’s Parishes, 149), at 70 Kensington Gardens Square in the presence of his son Maurice [death certificate] but according to the probate of his will at 2 Radnor Place Hyde Park.

**Dates:**  (1816/7-2 April 1910)

**Dates:**  (1867-6 Apr 1940)

##      William Crawley Yonge {#1631}

**Dates:**  (2 June 1795-26 Feb 1854)

##     William Coulthard Yonge {#1632}

**Dates:** (September-December 1859)  
**Description:** nephew of CMY

His maternal grandmother was born Mary Emma Coulthard.

## The Rev. Charles Burell Yonge {#1656}

**Dates:** (1866-1943)  
**Description:** Rector of Newton Ferrars, cousin of CMY  

He was the son of the Rev.

Duke Yonge of Puslinch and of Charlotte Cordelia Pode, who were both first cousins of CMY, on her mother\'s and father\'s sides respectively, and were each other\'s second cousins.

Charles Yonge married (1899) Catherine Ada Helena Bowen.

He is remembered for the collection of rare crocuses he naturalized in the churchyard at Newton Ferrars.

## Elizabeth Birt Alice Yonge {#1723}

**Dates:** (1799/1800-1863)  
**Description:** cousin-in-law of CMY  

Elizabeth (Holmes) Reed married, as her third husband, CMY\'s cousin Dr.

John Francis Duke Yonge, son of the Rev.

Duke Yonge of Antony, who was about 14 years her junior: they had three sons: Francis Arthur Holmes Yonge, James Frederick Moore Yonge, and Stephen Duke Yonge.

He became a Roman Catholic in the late 1840s, to the consternation of his family, but according to CMY, she did not. [ Her marriage, under the name Elizabeth Bird Alice Reed, is recorded in Brussels, 1839 by the IGI; advertisement for administration of estate of J.V.C.

Reed in the Morning Post 16 April 1864, 1]

She was the daughter of Richard Holmes, of Westcott, St.

Dominick, Cornwall, and Elizabeth Nash.

She was first married (18 November 1815), aged not quite 16, in the church at Antony, Cornwall, to Cavalie Shorthouse Mercer (1789-1819), with whom she had two children, Theodosia Alice Sterling Mercer (1817-1832) and Henrietta Fyers (Mercer) Muller (1818-1839).

He died in Bermuda, leaving her a widow of 19.

She remarried (1822) Captain John Reed (d. 1835) with whom she had at least six children, including Eliza Holmes Reed, who married Thomas C.

Watson, and John Vaughan Carden Reed (d. 1858) Lieutenant in the Royal Marine Light Infantry.

She had perhaps known the much younger John Francis Duke Yonge since his childhood, since he had been brought up in Antony.

Information from Mr Graeme Hicks.

## Stephen Duke Yonge {#2183}

**Dates:** (Coblentz 1844/5-1912)  
**Description:** third son of CMY\'s cousin Dr. [[person:1622]John Francis Duke Yonge]  

Stephen Yonge had emigrated to Melbourne, Australia, by 1864.

The Gentleman\'s Magazine (1866), 399 records the marriage (18 July 1866) \'At the Roman Catholic Cathdral, Plymouth, Stephen Duke Yonge, esq., of Plymstock, to Madeline Bartlet, fourth daughter of the late Lieut.-Col.George Smith, Bombay Native Infantry, of The Lodge, Plymton.\'
However he does not appear in the 1871 or later English censuses, and in 1897 CMY evidently thought he was in California.

According to the Probate Records the will was proved in 1873 of \'Madeline Bartlett Yonge (Wife of Stephen Duke Yonge) formerly of Ladye Park near Liskeard in the County of Cornwall but late of Lower Lake, Lake County California . . who died 19 November 1872 at Lower Lake\'.

According to data assembled by family genealogists at http://www.ilind.net/ancestry/jfdyDesc/p1.htm#i754, Stephen Yonge seems to have had two children.

## Charles Duke Yonge {#2409}

**Dates:** (1812-1891)  
**Description:** historian, cousin of CMY  

CMY never mentions this cousin, who was the eldest son of her [Eton uncle](../persons.html#1586), and some of whose long list of publications have sometimes been confused with some of hers.

The Standard (1 April 1837) records his appearance before the Insolvent Debtors Court in connection with a long list of debts, amounting to over £2000, which he was unable to pay.

He was described as the son of a widow who allowed him £250 a year, who had taken a first-class degree at Oxford, but had aspired \'to the reputation of fashionable men.\' This episode is not mentioned by the ODNB, which records his later career, but might have created prejudice against him in the family.

##      Caroline Young {#1633}

**Dates:**  (b.1816/17-after 1871 census)  
**Description:**  first cousin and ward of Charlotte Keble  

She married (20 Oct 1839) Rev.

Peter Young.

They had children James 7, John 5, William 4, Mary 2 and Elizabeth 1 in 1851 census; in 1871 George Edward 19 Frederick Coxwell 8, Mary Jane 22, Elizabeth Ann 21, Charlotte Lucy 17; in 1881 Mary Jane 32 and Charlotte L 27; the last two still living with their father in Lincoln in 1901. [Recollections of the Rev.

Peter Young, M.A., late Rector of North Witham, Lincolnshire and Canon of Lincoln, edited by his daughter (Grimsby: Albert Gait 1903), a pamphlet in London Library]

Scotland 1854/5), Anna Edith (b. 1856/7), Louisa Caroline (b. 1858/9) and Marion Jemima (b. 1859/60). [1861, 81 census, Recollections of the Rev.

Peter Young]
